claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in the specified single-phase solid-solution state has low hardness and strength.
The low hardness and strength are governed by rapid dynamic recovery during deformation.
Dislocations nucleate readily in this alloy.
Dislocations glide readily in this alloy.
Frequent cross-slip and dislocation annihilation limit dislocation pile-up and forest hardening.
The relevant starting material is equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in an as-cast or annealed, single-phase, relatively coarse-grained solid-solution state.
At low strain rates, dynamic recovery operates efficiently through glide, cross-slip, and annihilation.
Efficient dynamic recovery prevents the buildup of dislocation structures that would otherwise cause work hardening.
Increasing strain rate partially suppresses dynamic recovery.
Partial suppression of dynamic recovery at higher strain rates produces higher flow stress.
In-situ TEM straining will show rapid dislocation nucleation and extensive cross-slip and annihilation.
The deformed alloy will retain a relatively low forest-dislocation density at moderate strain.
Lower strain rates will produce lower yield stress, lower flow stress, and lower strain-hardening rates than higher strain rates.
Higher strain rates will produce greater dislocation accumulation.
The starting alloy has high plasticity despite low hardness and strength.
The proposed mechanism applies at room temperature under quasi-static to moderate strain rates while CoCrFeNiTi remains equimolar and single phase.
Changes in composition, phase stability, or test temperature may activate different deformation mechanisms.
Micropillar TEM observations may not directly translate to bulk mechanical behavior because of scale effects.
